Theme – Infrastructure 
 
Community Aspirations 
 
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For 
the Theme – Infrastructure, the following are the community aspirations: 
 
Transport & Parking 
 
The road network across the villages is in a poor  physical condition and a solution to the roads 
being susceptible and badly impacted by ground movement needs to be explored. 
 
The villages have a lack of footways; in the town the footways are narrow and are a challenge to 
navigate at certain times, such as on bin day. As the number of bins increases there needs to be 
exploration into different  solutions, solar  compacting  bins  for  example that  might  assist  in 
mitigating the size and number of bins on the footway. 
 
Ramsey town has high levels of on-street parking, and the town centre struggles with not having 
sufficient parking provision to meet the needs of shoppers and those who live and work within the 
town  centre. Opportunities  to  secure  additional  provision  and  access  to  cost-effective  public 
electric vehicle charging also need to be explored. 
 
Accessibility/Connectivity 
 
Connectivity between the villages is poor, as is connectivity between the villages and the town. 
The  geographic  isolation  of  the  parish  means  that  the  provision  of  good  phone  and  internet 
connection  /  signal/  coverage is  vital. Local  support  for  the services  in  town – dentists, GP’s, 
district nurses, physios etc. needs to occur. This can include support for these services to diversify 
their  health  offer  and provide  the  opportunity  for  outreach  hospital services  where  feasible. 
Hospital facilities are difficult to get to if you do not drive.  
 
Balanced development is wanted to support a thriving community of all ages. Including support 
for family members to stay in the area throughout their lives; thereby keeping and supporting the 
local  connection which  is  a  vital  component  of  the  community  spirit  which  was  evident  in  the 
public consultation responses. Employment opportunities with small start-ups and industrial units 
as well as shops is important. 
 
Ensuring  that  we  signpost  services  for  those  with  disabilities,  children  and  the  elderly is  an 
important aspiration. An aging community needs support for aspects like the community bus/ cars 
to provide connection to the larger towns and cities. 
 
We recognise that the villages around Ramsey are growing and are bringing more traffic, shoppers 
and people wanting to access services in the town. Due to the poor accessibility and connectivity, 
new development results in use of the private car rather than active travel modes such as walking 
and cycling. It is a community aspiration to maintain the culture, the things that make the villages 
and town unique  and  the  community  feel.  Overall  rural  tourism  is  preferrable  and  more 
appropriate than housing to maintain that culture.

Development proposals will be supported where they demonstrate how opportunities for the use 
of sustainable modes of transport are maximised.  This should be achieved through maximising the 
potential  for  cycling  and  walking  throughout  the  site;  provision  of  safe  crossings; secure  cycle

and  existing  parts  of Ramsey and  further  afield  including Bury  and  Upwood  Airfield.  Where  a 
proposal  will  have  a  significant  impact  on  the  existing  transport  network  this  would  be  best 
demonstrated through a transport assessment. 
 
Development proposals should include recreational routes for pedestrians which link into existing 
and proposed green infrastructure in order to contribute to health and well-being. 
 
In  all  proposals  consideration  should  be  given  to  how  the  development  can  contribute to the

Policy 9 – Highway Impact 
 
 
Proposals  will be supported  where they  would  not  adversely  affect  the  local  highway  network. 
Where proposals would negatively  impact  on  the local highway  network,  contributions  will  be 
sought, where appropriate, through a Planning Obligation to minimise and mitigate those impacts 
associated with the development.  
 
Any new development which involves alterations to existing highways and the provision of new 
highways would be supported where it meets the following design criteria:  
• Provides suitable measures to accommodate traffic (including at peak times); 
• Improve the safety and attractiveness of the street scene; and 
• Integrate appropriate traffic-calming measures within the development. 
 
Development  should  incorporate  adequate dedicated on-site  provision  for  parking within  the 
curtilage  of  properties  or  in small and  well-overlooked parking  courts  or  similar. Development 
proposals which would result in the displacement of existing off-street parking provision to on-
street parking will not be supported. Proposals that incorporate car-free areas such as play streets 
would be supported. 
 
New development should incorporate adequate on-site provision for the storage and collection of 
refuse  bins. Where  appropriate  refuse  collection  storage  should  be  screened  and be easily 
accessible to the collection point. Where developers want to promote alternative or innovative 
methods of storage such as underground bin storage where viability and operational practicalities 
allow this would be supported; particularly where this improves the visual aspects of recycling and 
waste management for the benefit of the community. 
 
 
32. Rights of Way Network 
 
32.1 Ramsey covers a large area of countryside and as a consequence it would be expected that 
it may benefit from an extensive and well-used rights of way network. However, across the 
parish as a whole there are relatively limited public rights of 
way. It is possible to get from Ramsey Forty Foot and Ramsey 
Heights  to Ramsey.  Ramsey St Mary’s by contrast  has  no 
public rights of way.  
 
32.2 An effective rights of way network provides a dual role for 
recreation and for sustainable travel. Their recreational use 
makes an important contribution to health and well-being. 
The  areas  allocated  for  housing  are  distant  from  the  main 
services  and  facilities  in Ramsey. As  such  the right of  way 
network  contributes  to  accessibility  and  providing  the 
opportunity for sustainable travel using non-vehicle modes. 
The  Neighbourhood  Plan  looks  to  improve  and  extend  the 
rights of way network.  
 
32.3 Current provision for pedestrians and cyclists is not significant. Consultation identified the 
lack of  connection  between  the  villages  and  town  to be  an  issue. There  are  a  number  of 
footpaths and footways that pass through the town, including footways in the centre of the 
town that are narrow  and/or  are  in poor quality,  with  the  High  Street being  a  particular 
example. Narrow streets and on street parking also make cycling difficult and increase the 
feeling of danger, particularly for young people travelling to school.

Monitoring and Review 
 
34.1 Continual plan review is a fundamental element of the planning system. It is important to 
check that the plan is being implemented correctly, ensure that outcomes match objectives 
and to change the plan if they are not.  This Neighbourhood Plan will be carefully monitored 
by  the Town Council and  reviewed  if  it  becomes  apparent  that  the vision,  goals and 
objectives of the Plan are not being met.  
 
34.2 Monitoring  is  a  shared  responsibility  of  the Town Council  as  the  qualifying  body; 
Huntingdonshire  District  Council  as  the  Local  Planning  Authority;  and  users  of  the 
Neighbourhood Plan. The Town Council will consider the effectiveness of the policies and 
proposals  in  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  each  time  it  makes  representations  on  a  planning 
application;  alongside  seeking  views  on  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  at  each  Annual  Parish 
Meeting. The Town Council will request Huntingdonshire District Council to raise with it any 
issues  arising  out  of  the  development  management  process  in  determining  individual 
planning applications. Users of the Neighbourhood Plan are encouraged to make comments 
on monitoring of the Neighbourhood Plan to the Town Council at any point. 
 
34.3 The Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared to guide development up to 2046. It is unlikely 
that the Neighbourhood Plan will remain current and entirely relevant for  the entire plan 
period and may, in whole or in part, require some amendments before 2046. 
 
34.4 There are  a  number  of circumstances  under  which  a  partial  review  of  the  plan  may  be 
necessary, in accordance with best practice, the Town Council and its partners will consider 
undertaking a partial review of the Neighbourhood Plan no later than 5 years following its 
finalisation.

Affordable housing *: Housing for sale or rent, for those whose needs are not met by the market

] 
 
Amenity *: A positive element or elements that contribute to the overall character or enjoyment 
of an area. For example, open land, trees, historic buildings and the inter-relationship between 
them, or less tangible factors such as tranquillity. 
 
Ancient Woodland: An area that has been wooded continuously since at least 1600 AD. It includes 
ancient semi-natural woodland and plantations on ancient woodland sites (PAWS). 
 
Conservation (for heritage policy): The process of maintaining and managing change to a heritage 
asset in a way that sustains and, where appropriate, enhances its significance. 
 
Community  Infrastructure  Levy (CIL) *:  A  levy  allowing  local  authorities  to  raise  funds  from 
owners or developers of land undertaking new building projects in their area. 
 
Development plan: Is defined in section 38 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004, 
and includes adopted local plans, neighbourhood plans that have been made and published spatial 
development  strategies,  together  with  any  regional  strategy  policies  that  remain  in  force. 
Neighbourhood plans that have been approved at referendum are also part of the development 
plan, unless the local planning authority decides that the neighbourhood plan should not be made.  
 
Economic development *: Development, including those within the B and E Use Classes, public 
and community uses, and main town centre uses (but excluding housing development). 
 
Green  infrastructure: A  network  of  multi-functional  green  and  blue  spaces  and  other  natural 
features, urban and rural, which is capable of delivering a wide range of environmental, economic, 
health and wellbeing benefits for nature, climate, local and wider communities and prosperity.  
 
Heritage asset: A building, monument, site, place, area or landscape identified as having a degree 
of  significance  meriting  consideration  in  planning  decisions,  because  of  its  heritage  interest. 
Heritage  asset  includes  designated  heritage  assets  and  assets  identified  by the  local  planning 
authority (including local listing). 
 
Historic  environment:  All  aspects  of  the  environment  resulting  from  the  interaction  between 
people and places through time, including all surviving physical remains of past human activity, 
whether visible, buried or submerged, and landscaped and planted or managed flora. 
 
International,  national  and  locally  designated  sites  of  importance  for  biodiversity:  All 
international  sites  (Special  Areas of Conservation,  Special Protection  Areas,  and Ramsar  sites),

documents adopted under the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004. A local plan can consist 
of either strategic or non-strategic policies, or a combination of the two.  
 
Neighbourhood  plans: A  plan  prepared  by  a  parish  council  or  neighbourhood  forum  for  a 
designated neighbourhood area. In law this is described as a neighbourhood development plan in

decision making on planning applications. 
 
Open space: All open space of public value, including not just land, but also areas of water (such 
as rivers, canals, lakes and reservoirs) which offer important opportunities for sport and recreation 
and can act as a visual amenity.

contained in this Neighbourhood Plan or another document which forms part of the Development 
Plan. 
 
Planning condition: A condition imposed on a grant of planning permission (in accordance with 
the Town and Country Planning Act 1990) or a condition included in a Local Development Order or 
Neighbourhood Development Order. 
 
Planning obligation: A legally enforceable obligation entered into under section 106 of the Town 
and Country Planning Act 1990 to mitigate the impacts of a development proposal. 
 
Planning  Practice  Guidance  *: this  forms  the  overall  national  planning  practice  guidance  and 
advice  produced  by  the  Government  to  inform  the  making  of  Development  Plans  including 
Neighbourhood Plans and decision making on planning applications. 
 
Ramsar  sites:  Wetlands  of  international  importance,  designated  under  the  1971 Ramsar 
Convention. 
 
Rural exception sites: Small sites used for affordable housing in perpetuity where sites would 
not normally be used for housing. Rural exception sites seek to address the needs of the local 
community by accommodating households who are either current residents or have an existing 
family or employment connection. A proportion of market homes may be allowed on the site at 
the local planning authority’s discretion, for example where essential to enable the delivery of 
affordable units without grant funding. [Also see Policy LP 28 of the Local Plan] 
 
Scheduled Monument *: Those monuments that are given legal protection by being scheduled by 
Historic England.

Self-build and custom-build housing:  Housing built by an individual,  a group of individuals, or 
persons working with or for them, to be occupied by that individual. Such housing can be either 
market or  affordable housing. A legal definition, for  the purpose of applying the Self-build and 
Custom Housebuilding Act 2015 (as amended), is contained in section 1(A1) and (A2) of that Act. 
 
Setting of a heritage asset: The surroundings in which a heritage asset is experienced. Its extent 
is not fixed and may change as the asset and its surroundings evolve. Elements of a setting may 
make a positive or negative contribution to the significance of an asset, may affect the ability to 
appreciate that significance or may be neutral. 
 
Settlement  Boundary *: The  boundary  drawn  around  various  towns  and  villages  to  limit  new 
development and define the ‘built-up area’ of the settlement. Outside of the settlement boundary 
is considered to be the countryside. 
 
Significance (for heritage policy): The value of a heritage asset to this and future generations 
because  of  its  heritage  interest.  The  interest  may  be  archaeological,  architectural,  artistic  or 
historic. Significance derives not only from a heritage asset’s physical presence, but also from its 
setting.  For  World  Heritage  Sites,  the  cultural value described within each site’s Statement of 
Outstanding Universal Value forms part of its significance. 
 
Special  Areas  of  Conservation  (SAC):  Areas  defined  by  regulation  3  of  the  Conservation  of 
Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  which  have  been  given  special  protection  as  important 
conservation sites. 
 
Special  Protection  Areas  (SPA):  Areas  classified  under  regulation  15  of  the  Conservation  of 
Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  which  have  been  identified  as  being  of  international 
importance for the breeding, feeding, wintering or the migration of rare and vulnerable species 
of birds. 
 
Site  of  Special Scientific  Interest:  Sites designated  by  Natural  England  under  the  Wildlife  and 
Countryside Act 1981. 
 
Strategic Environmental Assessment: A procedure (set out in the Environmental Assessment of 
Plans and Programmes Regulations 2004) which requires the formal environmental assessment of 
certain plans and programmes which are likely to have significant effects on the environment. 
 
Supplementary planning documents: Documents which add further detail to the policies in the 
Local Plan. They can be used to provide further guidance for development on specific sites, or on 
particular  issues,  such  as  design.  Supplementary  planning  documents  are  capable  of  being  a 
material consideration in planning decisions but are not part of the development plan. 
 
Sustainable transport modes: Any efficient, safe and accessible means of transport with overall 
low  impact  on  the  environment,  including  walking  and  cycling,  low  and  ultra-low  emission 
vehicles, car sharing and public transport. 
 
Windfall sites: Sites not specifically identified in the development plan.

8 Foreword

On behalf of Ramsey Town Council, welcome to the Neighbourhood Plan for our Parish area which covers  the  settlements  of Ramsey;  Ramsey  Forty  Foot;  Ramsey  Heights;  Ramsey  Mereside  & Ramsey St Mary’s; together with the area of Ramsey Hollow & a small part of Pondersbridge.

The Neighbourhood Plan sets out the vision, objectives and policies to ensure that the town and the villages maintain their character, appearance and uniqueness over the period up to 2046; whilst helping to facilitate growth. The town is undergoing significant planned development, and the Neighbourhood Plan aims to ensure that the  planned  growth  respects  the  important  features  that  make our  communities distinctive.
The Neighbourhood Plan seeks to protect and enhance the natural and built environment of the parish which forms the character of where we live.

The Neighbourhood Plan has been drawn up by a Neighbourhood Plan Steering Group on behalf of Ramsey Town Council which is the designated body for the plan area and provided the funding and support  to  enable  the  plan  to  go  ahead. The Neighbourhood Plan  has  gone through  a  number  of stages including statutory public consultation and an Independent  Examination. The  Neighbourhood  Plan was  found  to  be  appropriate  by  the  Independent Examiner who published their report in late August 2026.

The   process now involves a   local   referendum requiring a majority ‘Yes’ vote of all those voting in the referendum for it to be accepted. In the event of a ‘Yes’ vote, Huntingdonshire District Council will proceed to ‘make’ the Neighbourhood Plan for the Parish of Ramsey.

The  Neighbourhood  Plan  sets  down  a  series  of planning    policies    which    will    form    part    of Huntingdonshire’s  wider  statutory  development plan.  The  Neighbourhood  Plan will  be  used  for determining   planning   applications   alongside the Huntingdonshire Local Plan.
It  is  intended  that  the  policies  will  be  reviewed periodically to monitor the cumulative effects of the policies  and,  if  necessary,  make  changes  to  keep them up to date and relevant.
So, our personal thanks to all those who have driven the process so far and thank you for taking the time to consider the Neighbourhood Plan.
Councillor Mrs Val Fendley Mayor of Ramsey Town Council
Sarah Mullineux Lead of the Neighbourhood Plan Steering Group

9 Introduction
1. Background

1.1 The Localism Act 2011 introduced a new type of Community Led Plan.  Communities now have the right to produce a Neighbourhood Plan, setting out policies on the development and use of land.  Developing a Neighbourhood Plan is a way for communities to play a greater role in determining the future of their area. A plan period of 2046 has been chosen to match the plan period of the emerging Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2046.

1.2 The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan forms part of the statutory Development Plan. This means that Huntingdonshire District Council will determine planning applications within the Parish in accordance with the development plan which includes this Neighbourhood Plan unless material planning considerations indicate otherwise (see section 38(6) 1 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004).

1.3 This Neighbourhood Plan is a Community Led Plan.  It has been  prepared  by a  Steering  Group  made  up  of local residents and councillors on behalf of the Town Council with professional   support.   It   has   been   informed   by   public participation and consultation firstly carried out informally in    2025 with    the    local    community. The    formal Neighbourhood  Plan  preparation  process will involve  two statutory  periods  of  public  consultation;  this  is  the  first statutory consultation to undertaken in 2026 as prescribed in Regulations 2 .

1.4 A Neighbourhood Plan is a planning document and is about the use and development of land. Neighbourhood planning gives communities more control over the future of their area by giving local people the chance to have their say on what happens where they live.

1.5 A neighbourhood   plan   can   establish   general   planning policies for  the development and use of land in a particular area. Plans can include local priorities, planning policies, proposals for improving an area or providing new facilities or infrastructure and allocation of key sites for development.

1.6 Neighbourhood planning  is  a  tool  to  promote  sustainable  growth  and  will  not  be  able  to prevent  development  in  an  area.  Neighbourhood  plans  can  only  include  proposals  for  an equal  (or  greater)  amount  of  growth  than  is  set  out  in  the  local  authority's  development plan. They must also accord with national planning policy
2. Sustainability Appraisal (SA) and Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA)

2.1 Every Neighbourhood  Plan  needs  to  consider  the  need  for  a  Sustainability  Appraisal (incorporating a Strategic Environmental Assessment) for the Neighbourhood Plan.  SA is a mechanism  for  considering  and  communicating  the  impacts  of  an  emerging  plan,  and potential alternatives in terms of key sustainability issues.

10 2.2 The Town Council considers that there will be no significant environmental effects arising from the Neighbourhood Plan. They have produced a SEA and HRA Screening Assessment for the Neighbourhood Plan which has demonstrated that a SEA is not required. Consequently, no SA incorporating an SEA has been undertaken for the Neighbourhood Plan.
3. National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF)

3.1 Throughout this  Neighbourhood  Plan  reference  is  made  to  the  National  Planning  Policy Framework (NPPF).  The NPPF sets out the government’s planning policies for England and how these are expected to be applied.  It was first published on 27 March 2012, with the NPPF version 3 against  which  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  was produced  and  examined being published in December 2024. It is also supplemented by Planning Practice Guidance.
3.2 The NPPF provides a framework to produce locally distinctive Neighbourhood Plans which reflect the needs and aspirations of the community.

3.3 The Government had consulted on a new draft NPPF 4 over the period from December 2025 to March 2026. The draft NPPF proposed for the first time there is a clear set of separate policies  for  both  plan-making  and  decision-making.  This  is  intended  to  achieve  three principal objectives, namely to:

• Ensure national planning policy is accessible and understandable for  everyone who uses it; • Establish  a  comprehensive  suite  of  national  policies  on  general  planning  matters which  will  apply  across  the  country,  to  avoid  these  matters  being  repeated  or deviated from in locally-produced plans; and • Make  the  policy  which  it  contains  more  ‘rules-based’  and  certain,  and  so  more capable of supporting timely and consistent.

3.4 The Neighbourhood Plan preparation did take account of the new draft NPPF as it gave a clear direction of travel. The Government then published the new NPPF 5 in mid-August 2026 shortly before  the  Independent  Examination  of  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  ended. The Government has incorporated policies  relating  to  traveller  sites, previously set  out  in Planning Policy for Traveller Sites, within the relevant chapters of the NPPF.

3.5 The Neighbourhood Plan contributes towards the achievement of sustainable development. More detail on the ways in which this Plan addresses sustainable development is included within the Basic Conditions Statement that accompanies the Plan.
4. Planning Practice Guidance

4.1 Planning Practice  Guidance 6 sets  out  the  government’s  advice  on  how  to  undertake neighbourhood planning within England. This is set out in detail within Section 41 of Planning Practice Guidance. Planning Practice Guidance also sets out national advice on a wide range of planning topics.

6. Background

12 6.2 All policies  within  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  should  be  read  in  conjunction  with  the Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036. When determining proposals for development, no policy will be applied in isolation and account will be taken of all relevant policies. Even if the proposed Local Government Reorganisation occurs,  the Development Plan will not change until any replacement Development Plan is adopted.
7. Relationship to Huntingdonshire Local Plan

7.1 The  Huntingdonshire Local Plan  to  2036 7 was adopted  in May 2019. Any  reference  in  this Neighbourhood  Plan  to  ‘Local  Plan’  or  ‘Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan’  means  the Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036.

7.2 The purpose of the Local Plan is to set out: • the strategy for development in the whole of Huntingdonshire; • policies for managing development; and • details of sites for development to meet the needs of Huntingdonshire.

7.3 The District Council is in the process of undertaking a Local Plan Update 8 to be known as the Huntingdonshire Local  Plan  to  2046.  The Preferred  Options  Draft  Local  Plan  to  2046 was published for consultation during November and December 2025. There is no obligation for a Neighbourhood Plan to be in general conformity with an emerging Local Plan; although it is sensible to look to ensure that inconsistency is avoided. Although, there is no certainty that  allocations  or  proposals  identified  in  the  Preferred  Options  Draft  Local  Plan  will  be carried forward into the later stages.

7.4 In broad terms the Preferred Options Draft Local Plan to 2046 9 looked to continue the same approach  to  the  settlement hierarchy.  Limited  additional  allocations for  housing  and employment are proposed at Upwood Airfield (in both Bury and Ramsey parishes) and on the north-eastern  and south-eastern sides  of  Ramsey  town. A  that  time  there were  two  main areas of consistency that need to be considered in the context of future general conformity between the emerging Neighbourhood Plan and the emerging Local Plan Review. These were in relation to a protected settlement break between Ramsey and Upwood Airfield/Bury, and the area between Ramsey Rural Museum and Ramsey 1940s Camp which the Neighbourhood Plan proposes as Local Green Space.

7.5 Any  reference  in  this  Neighbourhood  Plan  to  ‘Local  Plan Update’  means  the emerging Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to 2046. Huntingdonshire  District  Council  are scheduled  to publish the  Proposed  Submission  Local  Plan Update  to  2046 for  consultation  across September and October 2026. That will then need to be submitted to the Secretary of State which is anticipated to be in December 2026. Followed by the examination process during 2027, with adoption anticipated in 2028.

7.6 The Proposed Submission Local Plan Update to 2046 still proposes allocations for housing and employment at Upwood Airfield (in both Bury and Ramsey parishes) and on the south-eastern side  of  Ramsey  town. Together  with  a  housing  allocation  at  Ramsey  Forty  Foot on  the southern side.
7.7 Even if the proposed Local Government Reorganisation occurs, the Local Plan Update would still be likely to be completed by the new Council if appropriate.

13 8. Strategic policies for the purposes of neighbourhood planning

8.1 The system  of  neighbourhood  planning  allows Parish and  Town  Councils  to  produce neighbourhood plans to guide development at a local level. One of the requirements of such plans was that they should be in line with the 'strategic policies' of the adopted development plan for  the local area. Although, this legal requirement was removed in late March 2026 during  the  preparation  of  this Neighbourhood  Plan. As  preparation  started  with  this requirement in place, reference is still made to it.

8.2 Huntingdonshire District Council as the Local Planning Authority defines which policies are to  be  considered  'strategic'  with  regard  to  the production  of  a  neighbourhood plan. They consider that some of the policies and all the allocations within the Huntingdonshire Local Plan to  2036 are to be considered  'strategic'  for  the  purposes  of  neighbourhood  planning. 18 Vision
16.1 The following vision has been developed for the Neighbourhood Plan:

To  provide  a  planning  framework  and  policies  that  will result  in  sustainable  growth  for  the  local  community, ensuring  that  appropriate  infrastructure,  services  and facilities are provided whilst also conserving the distinct character of the town and villages that form the overall community of Ramsey.
Objectives
16.2 The following objectives have been set out for the Neighbourhood Plan:
(A) Promote sustainable development and infrastructure

• Collaborate through the production of development plans and the determination of planning applications  including  pre-application  engagement with  Huntingdonshire District  Council and  developers  of  individual  parcels to ensure  that growth  of  the Ramsey Spatial Planning Area delivers sustainable growth without resulting in further coalescence with Bury and Upwood Airfield. • Ensure that new development is of high-quality design, is built to a high sustainability standard and includes or contributes to open space and community facilities. • Ensure that the design and location of new development is resilient to the effects of climate change and flooding. • Ensure that new development integrates into the existing town or village including linking  all  developments  to  the  rest  of  the town  or village  with  footpaths,  where appropriate. • Locate new development such that current problems with congestion, parking and road safety are not exacerbated and, if possible, reduced.
(B) Conserve and enhance the built and natural environment

• Protect, enhance and conserve the open spaces; landscape; views; and biodiversity across the town and villages. • Use land efficiently and to preserve high quality agricultural land. • Conserve  and  enhance  the built environment  of  the town  and villages, including through  ensuring that  new  development  respects  or  enhances  the distinctive character and appearance of the area in which it is sited.
(C) Protect and develop the communities of Ramsey

• Protect  and  preserve  important community assets  including  its  local  services  and facilities by encouraging the retention and growth of community facilities. • Continue to improve the facilities on offer to support the local community, including through outreach services. • Continue to support community events.

Community Aspirations
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For the Theme – Community, the following are the community aspirations:
Community

The Town  Council  and  Neighbourhood Plan  want  to  support the  various  communities  that collectively  make  up  the  parish  of  Ramsey. A  vibrant  and flourishing community includes supporting families; encouraging the provision of places to live, work, stay and play; with suitable provision of housing including a local connection for housing and affordable housing.

The communities of Ramsey need suitable resilience to adapt to changing circumstances and be supported  to  allow  suitable  access  to  services  and  facilities  despite  the  relative  geographic isolation.

Resilience also needs to cater for ageing population needs; this includes the provision of specialist supported accommodation such as extra care housing or supported living schemes for people of all ages with care and support needs. Provision of adult mental health supported accommodation and  provision  for  adults  with  learning  disabilities  needs  to  be  provided  as  part  of  an  overall balanced and mixed community.
It is an aspiration to ensure that community clubs for  all ages are available and that access to adult education is available locally.

Adequate provision of services in proportion to the growth is imperative.  Additional services or replacement or extension of existing community buildings such as the library, community centre needs  to  be  factored  in. The  communities  want  a  holistic  and  joined  up  approach  so  that development,  infrastructure  and services  are  set  up  in  a  harmonious,  cohesive  and  sustainable way.
Education
Education needs to be fit for purpose and be well located; including being accessible safely for all ages by active travel methods including by foot and bicycle.

Suitable  and  adequate  early  years  provision to  meet  the  differing  needs  of  families.  Such  as through day nurseries, full day care, sessional provisional, childminders and wraparound care to provide breakfast and after school provision term-time between the hours of 8am and 6pm; need to be available in order to allow parents the opportunity to return to work. Additional capacity is required across  schools to meet demand. In terms of wider education, access to adult education should be available locally.

Such speculative development in addition to the allocated sites has the potential to undermine the strategic policies of the Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036 in terms of the distribution of housing across the district. It also has the potential to affect the distinctive character and separate identity of Ramsey and the adjacent village of Bury as separate and distinct settlements.

19.2 Ramsey  town is part of the ‘Ramsey Spatial Planning Area’ in Policy LP 2 - Strategy  for Development.  Policy  LP  7 - Spatial  Planning  Areas,  supports  development  where  it  is appropriately  located  within  a  built-up  area  of  an  identified  Spatial  Planning  Area settlement. The Local Plan does not specify any specific housing requirement for the villages of Ramsey Forty Foot; Ramsey Heights; Ramsey Mereside & Ramsey St Mary’s; nor for  the
Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan (Referendum Version)

31 part of Pondersbridge which are all deemed as ‘small settlements’ in the Local Plan. There is an overall allowance for windfall development to come forward across the collective 73 small settlements in the Local Plan.

19.3 The Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036 does not identify a settlement boundary for these villages; instead, it  moves  to  use  of a definition of ‘built-up area’. Policy  LP 9 – Small Settlements, supports development where it is appropriately located within a built-up area of a small settlement. This is what is known as windfall development as it relates to housing coming forward on sites not specifically allocated for housing.

19.4 A settlement boundary is proposed for the town of Ramsey. As this will be contiguous with the  built-up  area  of  the  adjoining  village  of  Bury in  some  places;  as  explained in the Settlement  Boundary  Methodology document we have  ensured that  consistency  with  the settlement  boundary  in  the  Bury Neighbourhood Plan has  taken place.

19.5 For Ramsey  Forty  Foot;  Ramsey  Heights;  Ramsey  Mereside  & Ramsey  St  Mary’s a settlement  boundary  is proposed  to  be identified to  define  the  ‘built-up  area’ as  referred  to  in  the Huntingdonshire   Local   Plan   to   2036. The   small   part   of Pondersbridge  in  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area  on  its  own  falls below  the  size  parameter  of  30  homes  in  the  Local  Plan  to  be identified  as  a  built-up  area. Therefore,  as  explained  in  the Settlement   Boundary   Methodology document,   no   settlement boundary   for   Pondersbridge   has been established   in   the Neighbourhood Plan.

19.6 The settlement boundary  of these  settlements serves a  specific purpose  in  that  it  is  intended  to direct the  growth  of  the settlement and  enable development  to  take  place  in  a  coherent manner,  maintaining  the  structure  and  form  of  the  existing  settlement  geography as  the Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036 envisages.  In  addition,  the  boundary  will  protect  the landscape setting of the villages.

19.7 The Huntingdonshire Townscape SPD for Ramsey identifies wording that says, ‘Reflect the existing built forms and local relationship with the street in any new development’. Policy 1 of the NP refers to taking into account the existing built form, layout and structure of the surrounding area.

19.8 This is intended to cover the wide array of factors that contribute to the distinctiveness of how a place looks, works and functions. In terms of structure, we mean factors such as the configuration,  the    arrangement  of  the  built  elements  in  a  particular  form,  figure,  or combination.

19.9 The National Design Guide suggests that structure can be a separate consideration to built form or layout.  For  example,  M2 of National Design Guide looks for  a clear structure and hierarchy of streets. It goes on to identify in relation to Layout that: “A layout shows how routes and blocks of development are arranged and relate to one another to create streets, open spaces and buildings. It defines: the structure or settlement pattern; the grain, or the pattern of development blocks and plots; and the broad distribution of different uses, and their densities or building heights.”
19.10 The National Design Guide also refers to the structure of blocks and routes that this creates; as well as open space, its location and structure need careful consideration.

38 20. Protected Settlement Break

20.1 Parts of Bury immediately abut the town of Ramsey, together with Upwood Airfield the two settlements form the Ramsey Spatial Planning Area. The Upwood Airfield area actually falls mostly in the Parish of Bury, with the northern part partly in the Parish of Ramsey and the western side in the Parish of Upwood. Parish Boundaries

20.2 The Parish boundary between Bury and Ramsey was established before much of the growth and development occurred. Over time a degree of coalescence between Bury and Ramsey has already occurred. The northern part of Bury around Signal Road is contiguous with the main  part  of  Ramsey,  as  such  although  spatially  part  of  Bury, it  physically  and  visually appears  as  an  extension  to  Ramsey.  The  two  settlements  are  however  two  distinct communities and are in two separate but contiguous Parishes.

20.2 The inter-relationship between Ramsey and Bury can be considered in relation to the two broad areas of: 1. East of the B1040; and 2. West of the B1040. As the B1040 for part of its length  forms  the Parish  boundary on  the  north-south  alignment,  this  provides  a  logical feature to choose as the central point to work from in order to undertake an assessment.

20.4 East of the B1040 - There are in fact no gaps remaining between the two Parishes of Ramsey and Bury to the east of the B1040. However, there is a gap between the northern part of Bury around Signal Road and the main part of Bury village. This remaining gap is the only visual and physical separation between the main cores of Bury and Ramsey. Consequently, the Bury Neighbourhood Plan has identified this as a Protected Settlement Break as the only gap remaining to prevent the complete coalescence of Ramsey and Bury.

39 20.5 The importance of the gap between Low Bury and White Arches on Bury Road was confirmed in appeal APP/H0520/W/16/3155400 which was dismissed in November 2016. Ramsey and Bury  have  already  coalesced  in  part  over  past  decades,  this  means  that  the  remaining physical and visual breaks that remain are even more important to protect. Land to the east of Bury Road between Low Bury and White Arches along with the land to the rear running back  to  the  golf  course  was  deemed  important  to  retain  as  undeveloped  to  prevent coalescence. Consequently,  that  area  became  a  protected  settlement  break  in  the  made Bury Neighbourhood Plan. There is no need for the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan to do anything further in this area to prevent coalescence.

20.6 West of the B1040 - Bury has grown, including through the recent development of Longland Crescent  to  the  west  of  Upwood  Road.  Ramsey  has  grown,  including  through  the  recent development of Frost Way and Stonemason Way. This recent housing development has led to the greater threat of coalescence on the western side between Ramsey, Bury and Upwood Airfield. There is a wedge of countryside remaining between the northern side of Upwood Airfield,  the  western  side  of  Longland  Crescent  and  the  southern  side  of housing  on  the south-western fringe of the town of Ramsey.

20.7 Given  that  the  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036  proposes  that  the  ‘Ramsey  Spatial Planning Area’ has allocations for 895 homes and 2 hectares of employment land there is a real threat that unchecked growth could lead to further coalescence between Ramsey and Bury.  The  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to  2036  does  not  include  any policy  to prevent  the coalescence of Ramsey and Bury, although the Bury Neighbourhood Plan does. In terms of consistency,  it  is  appropriate  for  the  Ramsey  Neighbourhood  Plan  to  also  secure  this important community objective of retaining the distinct settlements of Ramsey and Bury.

20.8 There  is  also  the  potential  through  further  urban  extension  for  development  on  Upwood Airfield to lead to coalescence on the western side between Ramsey and Bury. Part of the northern part of Upwood Airfield lies within Ramsey Parish, although if developed spatially this area would effectively operate as part of Upwood Airfield. The allocations at Upwood Airfield  as  a  whole  visually  and  spatially appears  to  be part  of  Bury.  The  northern side  of  the  Airfield  in  this  area  is  rather distinctively  formed by  the  former  runway and  the  hedgerow  and  treed  boundary.  To the   north   of   this   is   a   wedge-shaped agricultural  field  that  currently  provides  a visual  and  physical  separation  in  the  built form between  Ramsey and Bury including Upwood  Airfield.  The  area  has  a  width  of around  130m  at  its  eastern  end  rising  to around 230m at the western end.
20.9 The  emerging  Local  Plan Update  to  2046 29

proposes to allocate the northern side of the Airfield  including  the  area formed  by  the  former  runway up  to the  hedgerow  and  treed boundary as Bury 3: RAF Upwood - Phase 3. This proposed allocation would be for a mixed- use  development  comprising  of  commercial  development  and  open  space  comprising  170 homes and about 11.5 ha of land for green infrastructure. This emerging allocation in the Local Plan Update to 2046 would bring built development on Upwood Airfield closer to the existing built development in Ramsey. Leaving just a single field that would prevent Ramsey and  Bury  completely  coalescing. Development  pressure  from  windfall  proposals  has  been significant in the Ramsey Spatial Area and is likely to continue for some time given the fact that Huntingdonshire does not have a demonstrable 5-year housing land supply.

40 20.10 Retaining  a  physical  and  visual  separation  in  this  area  would  be  important  to  retain  the distinct  separate  identity  of  Ramsey  and  Bury.  The  principle  of  preventing  further coalescence  between  the  two  settlements  has  been  established  in  the  made  Bury Neighbourhood  Plan.  As  such  it  has  been  found  to  be  an  appropriate  strategy  by  the Independent Examiner who undertook the examination of the Bury Neighbourhood Plan. It is important that adjoining Neighbourhood Areas have regard to cross boundary issues in the interest of consistency and so as not to undermine other parts of the Development Plan.

20.11 Consequently, it is considered to be necessary and appropriate in the Ramsey Neighbourhood Plan to set out a suitable policy approach to prevent further coalescence between Ramsey and  Bury.  As  such  a protected settlement  break  between  Ramsey  and  the  planned  urban edge of Upwood Airfield is therefore included in the Neighbourhood Plan. This is important to protect distinct identities of Ramsey and Bury as separate settlements.

20.12 Although  the  northern  end  of  the airfield  is  not currently  allocated  for  development,  it  is  an integral  part  of  the  wider  airfield  that  has  been identified for strategic growth in the Local Plan to 2036.  In  the  Land  Availability  Assessment  (LAA), the  site  on  the  northern  end  of  the  airfield  is known as Bury 7: RAF Upwood - Phase 3, Bury. In the  LAA,  Huntingdonshire  have  identified  that Bury 7 would be suitable for future development. Given   its   inter-relationship   to   the   existing development  on  Upwood  Airfield,  without  pre- determining  future  decisions;  it  is  considered reasonable to take the position that development continuing  on  the  airfield  is likely  to  occur. The Local Plan to 2046 is considering it as an emerging allocation now known as allocation ‘Bury 3’.

20.13 The  protected  settlement  break  forms  an  important  green  corridor  which  would  assist  in retaining the identity of the two existing settlements. It also provides opportunities for new green  infrastructure  and/or  biodiversity  enhancement  to  support  the  delivery  of  the strategic allocations. It is considered that the edge of the former Upwood airfield runway forms  an  existing  defensible  boundary  that  is  more  appropriate  to  form  the  southern boundary  of  the  protected  settlement  break,  rather  than  the  current  allocated  site boundaries which are further south. The northern and eastern boundaries of the protected settlement  break  is  to  be  the  existing  and  planned  current  edge  of  the  built-up  area  of Ramsey and Bury respectively.
20.14 More information on the importance of the Protected Settlement Break is contained in the Settlement Boundary Methodology document.

21.1 Community Facilities is  a  generic  term  used  for  community  infrastructure,  services  and facilities. As a town,  Ramsey has a wider range of community facilities than the villages. Ramsey Town Council provides and hosts a number of community services 30 . Ramsey is  also  blessed  to  have community  organisations  including  the  Ramsey  Neighbourhoods Trust 31 .

Policy 3 – Community Facilities

Development  proposals  that  result  in  the  improvement/enhancement of existing community facilities including meeting/event spaces (such as village halls or community centres); play areas; leisure/recreation/sports   facilities; allotments; education facilities (pre-schools/nurseries, primary  schools,  secondary  school or  adult/community  education); churches; library;  Ramsey Rural  Museum;  Ramsey  1940s Camp; cemeteries/burial  grounds; or small-scale  local retail facilities in  the  villages will  be  supported subject  to  their compliance  with other  development plan policies.

Development proposals that result in the provision of new community facilities both within and outside  of  but  adjacent  to  the  settlement  boundary of Ramsey; Ramsey  Forty  Foot; Ramsey Heights; Ramsey Mereside; and Ramsey St Mary’s will be supported subject to their compliance with other development plan policies; provided the scale is commensurate with size of facility to meet  the  needs of the  respective settlement and  where  relevant  the catchment  hinterland. The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For the Theme – Heritage & Environment, the following are the community aspirations:
Heritage & Tourism

The parish is home to a wealth of heritage assets, and the historic environment has been identified through public consultation as being of particular importance to local residents. 24. Natural Environment

24.1 Most  of  the parish  of Ramsey is rural  and contains  substantial  areas  of  farmland  which contributes  significantly  to  the  character  of  the parish  and  the  setting  of  the town  and villages.

24.2 There is a need to assess the likelihood of proposals or policies within a Neighbourhood Plan having a significant effect on the ‘National Sites Network’ consisting of areas designated as Special Areas of Conservation (SAC) or Special Protection Areas (SPA’s). Consideration of the internationally designated Ramsar sites is also necessary; many Ramsar sites are also SACs or  SPAs. In  the  vicinity  of the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area  the ‘National Sites Network’ of interest  are  the Orton  Pit  SAC  (Peterborough); Nene  Washes  SPA/Ramsar (East  of Peterborough);   Ouse   Washes   SAC/SPA/Ramsar (North-west   of   Ely);   Portholme   SAC (Huntingdon/Godmanchester); and Fenland SAC/Woodwalton Fen Ramsar.
24.3 The  closest  to  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  area is  the Fenland  SAC/Woodwalton  Fen  Ramsar which immediately abuts the south-west corner of the parish near Ramsey Heights.

24.4 SACs  were  previously  classified  in  accordance  with  EC  Directive  92/43/EEC  on  the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora (the Habitats Directive). Article 3  of  this  Directive  requires  the  establishment  of  a  European  network  of  important high‐ quality  conservation  sites  that  will  make  a  significant  contribution  to  conserving  the  189 habitat types and 788 species identified in Annexes I and II of the Directive. These sites are now  designated  under  the  Conservation  of  Habitats  and  Species  Regulations  2017  (as amended).

24.5 SPAs  were  sites  first  classified  in  accordance  with  Article  4  of  the  EC  Directive  on  the conservation of wild birds (79/409/EEC), more commonly known as the Birds Directive. They were classified for rare and vulnerable birds, listed in Annex I to the Birds Directive, and for regularly occurring migratory species. These SPA sites are now designated under the Wildlife

60 &  Countryside  Act  1981  (as  amended)  and  the  Conservation  (Natural  Habitats,  &  c.) Regulations 2010 (as amended).

24.6 Ramsar Sites are designated under the International Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat (the Ramsar Convention, Iran 1971 and amended by  the  Paris  Protocol  1992).  Although Ramsar  Sites are not protected in law by domestic  UK  legislation  as  a  matter  of policy   government, has   decreed   that unless   otherwise   specified   procedures relating  to  SPAs  and  SACs  will  also  apply to Ramsar Sites.

24.7 The    Habitats    Regulation    Assessment screening identifies that the Neighbourhood  Plan  proposals  would  not individually  or  cumulatively  result  in  any potential    significant    effects    on    any designated site.

24.8 The plan area contains no National Nature Reserves (NNR), Woodwalton Fen is also a NNR in addition to being a SAC and Ramsar  site. The other nearest NNR are at Upwood Meadows around 2km to the south-west and Holme Fen around 2km to the west of Ramsey St Mary’s. The Plan area contains no Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs). Woodwalton Fen is also a SSSI in addition to being an NNR, SAC and Ramsar site; Holme Fen is also a SSSI as well as being an NNR. Warboys  and  Wistow  Woods  SSSI  lies around  3km  to  the  south  of  Ramsey (town).

24.9 There are impact zones defined around the various designated sites to identify what scale of different types of development need consultation with Natural England. This principally impacts  on  Ramsey  Heights  and  Ramsey  St  Mary’s,  although  the  impact  zones  do  extend further across the Parish. These impact zones are shown in Appendix 1.

24.10 In  terms  of County  level  locally  designated  sites (County  Wildlife  Sites),  the  plan  area contains Ramsey Heights Nature Reserve and Reservoir East of Park Farm which lies north- east of Ramsey towards Ramsey Hollow.

24.11 The Great Fen Project Area extends into the western part of the parish near Ramsey Heights and Ramsey St Mary’s. The Great Fen Landscape & Visual Setting boundary extends across the western part of the parish, covering land west of Ugg Mere Court Road in Ramsey Heights and west of the B1040 in Ramsey St Mary’s.

24.12 The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS 44 ) is a bold new plan to revive and protect nature across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. It’s a locally driven, government-backed initiative that maps out where and how we can restore habitats, boost biodiversity, and reconnect people with the natural world, from countryside to city parks.

26.2 Surface  water  flooding  potential  affects  much  of  the  parish  of  Ramsey.  Surface  water flooding  is  a  matter  to  be  taken  into  account  in  the  planning  application  process 49 . The Neighbourhood Plan alongside the Local Plan and the NPPF strives to promote sustainable drainage techniques (SuDS).

26.3 Fluvial (river) flooding and surface water flooding risks change over  time, in part at least due to the impact of climate change. Developers when designing surface water systems have to design them with an allowance for climate change 50 . During December 2020 there were a large volume of flood incidents across Cambridgeshire, Ramsey was affected. The Lead Local Flood Authority (LLFA) undertook a statutory flood investigation and produced the relevant report 51 .

26.4 SuDS   are   an   approach   to   managing surface  water  run-off  which  seeks  to mimic  natural  drainage  systems  and retain  water  on  or  near  the  site  as opposed     to     traditional     drainage approaches which involve piping water off  site  as  quickly  as  possible.  SuDS offer    significant    advantages    over conventional piped drainage systems in reducing  flood  risk  by  attenuating  the rate and quantity of surface water run- off from a site, promoting groundwater recharge, and improving water quality, biodiversity and amenity. The LLFA would particularly support above-ground open SuDS such as wetlands, attenuation basins, ponds and swales as they provide additional amenity and biodiversity benefits.

26.5 Opportunities for increasing biodiversity at opportunity sites and in the protected settlement breaks are  discussed  within  the  Neighbourhood  Plan. There  is  a potential  for  increasing biodiversity through the use of SuDS features such as attenuation basins, ponds and swales in these circumstances.

The verdant and undeveloped nature  of  the  area  contributes  strongly  to  the  character  and  appearance  of  this  part  of  the Conservation Area.

The  land  is  abutted  on  both  sides  by  the Ramsey Rural Museum and the Ramsey 1940s Camp. It  has  historical  significance  through helping  both  of  those  attractions  tell  the story of the history of the town through the various events hosted on the land.

This  space  is  an  integral  part  of  Ramsey’s heritage.  Currently, the field is used for the maximum allowable events throughout the year. It links the Rural Museum and the Ramsey 1940s Camp  and  allows  for  highly  successful  joint  ventures  as  well  as  solo  events.  Without  it,  large community and nationally recognised events will no longer be able to occur causing loss of funding for both the Ramsey 1940s Camp and Ramsey Rural Museum. This could jeopardise the viability of both sites.

Historically, the side of the Museum protruding into the field was identified as an historic track and is adjacent to  what  is  believed  to  be  the  boundary  of  the  Abbey precinct 53 . There is also a possibility of ordinance from the Ramsey 1940s Camp from when it was a searchlight facility during World War II.  The area of the Camp was used during World War I, but documentation associated with  that  appears  to  be  sealed,  possibly  under  the Official Secrets Act.

The area is effectively an events space and showground where  a  significant  number  of  public  events  are  held. These  events  are  integral  to  the  cultural,  social  and  economic  life  of  the  community,  local businesses and attractions. Events held include the 1940s Weekend, the Fen Fair, Country Fair and Plough Day, Ramsey Steam & Fire Show. These events can have up to 3,500 people attending. The area is also used for other events including Dog Shows and Scooter Rallies.

The waterway has a natural beauty although further enhancement of the mooring would improve the function and overall recreational purpose without harming the overall beauty of this area. 82 Theme – Infrastructure
Community Aspirations
The Neighbourhood Plan includes community aspirations for each themed section of the Plan. For the Theme – Infrastructure, the following are the community aspirations:
Transport & Parking
The road network across the villages is in a poor  physical condition and a solution to the roads being susceptible and badly impacted by ground movement needs to be explored.

The villages have a lack of footways; in the town the footways are narrow and are a challenge to navigate at certain times, such as on bin day. As the number of bins increases there needs to be exploration into different  solutions, solar  compacting  bins  for  example that  might  assist  in mitigating the size and number of bins on the footway.

Ramsey town has high levels of on-street parking, and the town centre struggles with not having sufficient parking provision to meet the needs of shoppers and those who live and work within the town  centre. Opportunities  to  secure  additional  provision  and  access  to  cost-effective  public electric vehicle charging also need to be explored.
Accessibility/Connectivity

Connectivity between the villages is poor, as is connectivity between the villages and the town. The  geographic  isolation  of  the  parish  means  that  the  provision  of  good  phone  and  internet connection  /  signal/  coverage is  vital. Local  support  for  the services  in  town – dentists, GP’s, district nurses, physios etc. needs to occur. This can include support for these services to diversify their  health  offer  and provide  the  opportunity  for  outreach  hospital services  where  feasible. Hospital facilities are difficult to get to if you do not drive.

Balanced development is wanted to support a thriving community of all ages. Including support for family members to stay in the area throughout their lives; thereby keeping and supporting the local  connection which  is  a  vital  component  of  the  community  spirit  which  was  evident  in  the public consultation responses. Employment opportunities with small start-ups and industrial units as well as shops is important.

Ensuring  that  we  signpost  services  for  those  with  disabilities,  children  and  the  elderly is  an important aspiration. An aging community needs support for aspects like the community bus/ cars to provide connection to the larger towns and cities.

We recognise that the villages around Ramsey are growing and are bringing more traffic, shoppers and people wanting to access services in the town. Due to the poor accessibility and connectivity, new development results in use of the private car rather than active travel modes such as walking and cycling. It is a community aspiration to maintain the culture, the things that make the villages and town unique  and  the  community  feel.  Overall  rural  tourism  is  preferrable  and  more appropriate than housing to maintain that culture.

30.2 Ramsey and the surrounding villages are classed as a rural area, there are high levels of car ownership  and  reliance  on  the  car  to  maintain  access  to  key  services. Some  87.7%  of households  in  the  parish  of  Ramsey have  one or  more  cars/vans,  with almost  half  of  the households having two, three or more cars/vans. In addition, high house prices and lack of affordable housing has led to more people travelling further to work, with the average length of commute in Ramsey greater than the national average. 30.3 The  Huntingdonshire  Local  Plan  to 2036  contains  Policy  LP  16  which indicates that new development will be  expected  to  contribute  to  an enhanced  transport  network  that supports an increasing proportion of journeys    being    undertaken    by sustainable travel modes.

30.4 Access    to    high    quality    public transport  is  known  to  be  hugely beneficial  to  improving  access  to services for  those members of society who cannot,  for a variety of reasons, access a car. This is particularly acute in rural areas such as Ramsey where distances between households and essential services are often large, making walking and cycling less practical than in urban areas. The villages in the parish are reliant upon Ramsey town for many higher order services and facilities. However, the town doesn’t provide all essential services and journeys to larger settlements  such  as  Peterborough or  Huntingdon  are  necessary,  for  example to  access hospital services, higher education and many public services. The Town Council alongside the  Ramsey  Neighbourhood Trust 64 does  look  to  support  the  provision  of  outreach public services to improve accessibility.

30.5 It  has  recently  been  announced  that  there  will  be  a  new  direct  bus  service (X31) from Upwood, Bury and Ramsey to Peterborough from January 2026. This will be operated under the new Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority contract 65 .

30.6 The geographic nature of the parish makes it difficult for residents of the villages to access the services and facilities in Ramsey town centre by walking and cycling. The distances in combination with the lack of footways and uneven road surfaces due to the fenland geology are barriers to walking and cycling.

In addition, active travel can offer a convenient, accessible and affordable way to move more for shorter journeys. Active  travel  and sustainable  travel  modes not  only  positively  contribute  to addressing climate change but also can assist in maintaining a healthy community.

Unfortunately, traffic management is not an issue over which the Town Council has direct control. Most of the traffic originates outside the parish. As a consequence, traffic management cannot be easily addressed by this Neighbourhood  Plan.  However,  the Town  Council will  seek  to  support road  safety improvements around the plan area.

30.3 As part of the overall approach, the Neighbourhood Plan can support and ensure that new development  does  not  adversely  affect  the  highway  network; or  that  where  it  does, contributions through    a    Planning Obligation address     the     impacts appropriately. However, a Planning Obligation can only be sought where it meets the relevant tests; namely: it is necessary  to  make  the  development acceptable   in   planning   terms;   is directly  related  to  the  development; and is fairly and reasonably related in scale   and   kind. In   some cases, Cambridgeshire   County   Council   is seeking  more  direct  off-site  delivery of highway improvements, i.e. rather than paying the County Council a fee the  developer  will  undertake  the  works  in  the highway  directly. As such  in  some  cases  a planning  condition  may  be  the  appropriate  implementation  measure.  In  some cases, Community Infrastructure Levy monies will cover highway improvements.

30.4 The  policy  includes  reference  to the  storage  and  collection  of  refuse  bins as  where insufficient on-site provision is made this can result in a highway impact. This impact involves bins blocking pedestrian use of footways that can lead to pedestrian and vehicle conflict. The Cambridgeshire RECAP Waste Management Design Guide SPD 72 sets out advice on access, maximum travel distances, number of bins per property type etc. and takes into account the Council’s  Waste  Collection  Policies. The  policy looks  to provide  the  opportunity  for developers to promote alternative or innovative methods of storage such as underground bin storage,  for  example on larger sites if viability and operational practicalities support this approach  in  a development. Alternative  or  innovative  methods of storage could have the added benefit of improving the visual aspects of recycling and waste management for the benefit of the community, particularly where smaller dwellings are concentrated, and the provision of wheeled bins may be less desirable.

30.5 Where parking courts are proposed, care needs to be taken. These spaces often suffer from poor  natural surveillance, limited  overlooking  and  can  become  unsafe or underused.  It  is recommended in the policy that parking courts should only be used where they are small, well-overlooked,   incorporate   high   quality   and   subtle   use   of materials,   integrated landscaping and trees. The HDC Design Guide SPD 2017 on page 89 provides more detailed advice.

Policy 9 – Highway Impact

Proposals  will be supported  where they  would  not  adversely  affect  the  local  highway  network. Where proposals would negatively  impact  on  the local highway  network,  contributions  will  be sought, where appropriate, through a Planning Obligation to minimise and mitigate those impacts associated with the development.

Any new development which involves alterations to existing highways and the provision of new highways would be supported where it meets the following design criteria: • Provides suitable measures to accommodate traffic (including at peak times); • Improve the safety and attractiveness of the street scene; and • Integrate appropriate traffic-calming measures within the development.

Development  should  incorporate  adequate dedicated on-site  provision  for  parking within  the curtilage  of  properties  or  in small and  well-overlooked parking  courts  or  similar. Development proposals which would result in the displacement of existing off-street parking provision to on- street parking will not be supported. Proposals that incorporate car-free areas such as play streets would be supported.

New development should incorporate adequate on-site provision for the storage and collection of refuse  bins. Where  appropriate  refuse  collection  storage  should  be  screened  and be easily accessible to the collection point. Where developers want to promote alternative or innovative methods of storage such as underground bin storage where viability and operational practicalities allow this would be supported; particularly where this improves the visual aspects of recycling and waste management for the benefit of the community.
32. Rights of Way Network

32.1 Ramsey covers a large area of countryside and as a consequence it would be expected that it may benefit from an extensive and well-used rights of way network. However, across the parish as a whole there are relatively limited public rights of way. It is possible to get from Ramsey Forty Foot and Ramsey Heights  to Ramsey.  Ramsey St Mary’s by contrast  has  no public rights of way.

32.2 An effective rights of way network provides a dual role for recreation and for sustainable travel. Their recreational use makes an important contribution to health and well-being. The  areas  allocated  for  housing  are  distant  from  the  main services  and  facilities  in Ramsey. As  such  the right of  way network  contributes  to  accessibility  and  providing  the opportunity for sustainable travel using non-vehicle modes. The  Neighbourhood  Plan  looks  to  improve  and  extend  the rights of way network.

32.3 Current provision for pedestrians and cyclists is not significant. Consultation identified the lack of  connection  between  the  villages  and  town  to be  an  issue. There  are  a  number  of footpaths and footways that pass through the town, including footways in the centre of the town that are narrow  and/or  are  in poor quality,  with  the  High  Street being  a  particular example. Narrow streets and on street parking also make cycling difficult and increase the feeling of danger, particularly for young people travelling to school.

Monitoring and Review

34.1 Continual plan review is a fundamental element of the planning system. It is important to check that the plan is being implemented correctly, ensure that outcomes match objectives and to change the plan if they are not.  This Neighbourhood Plan will be carefully monitored by  the Town Council and  reviewed  if  it  becomes  apparent  that  the vision,  goals and objectives of the Plan are not being met.

34.2 Monitoring  is  a  shared  responsibility  of  the Town Council  as  the  qualifying  body; Huntingdonshire  District  Council  as  the  Local  Planning  Authority;  and  users  of  the Neighbourhood Plan. The Town Council will consider the effectiveness of the policies and proposals  in  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  each  time  it  makes  representations  on  a  planning application;  alongside  seeking  views  on  the  Neighbourhood  Plan  at  each  Annual  Parish Meeting. The Town Council will request Huntingdonshire District Council to raise with it any issues  arising  out  of  the  development  management  process  in  determining  individual planning applications. Users of the Neighbourhood Plan are encouraged to make comments on monitoring of the Neighbourhood Plan to the Town Council at any point.

34.3 The Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared to guide development up to 2046. It is unlikely that the Neighbourhood Plan will remain current and entirely relevant for  the entire plan period and may, in whole or in part, require some amendments before 2046.

34.4 There are  a  number  of circumstances  under  which  a  partial  review  of  the  plan  may  be necessary, in accordance with best practice, the Town Council and its partners will consider undertaking a partial review of the Neighbourhood Plan no later than 5 years following its finalisation.

35.1 The majority of the glossary is copied from the NPPF to ensure consistency 76 . The terms set out below are either included within the Neighbourhood Plan or are within parts of the NPPF or the Huntingdonshire Local Plan to 2036 that is referred to in the Neighbourhood Plan.

Affordable housing *: Housing for sale or rent, for those whose needs are not met by the market (including housing that provides a subsidised route to home ownership and/or is for essential local workers); and which complies with one or more of the following categories: affordable housing for rent;  starter  homes; discounted  market  sales  housing;  and  other  affordable  routes  to  home ownership including shared ownership, relevant equity loans, other low cost homes for sale (at a price equivalent to at least 20% below local market value) and rent to buy (which includes a period of intermediate rent). [Note a more detailed definition is included in the NPPF 77 ]

Amenity *: A positive element or elements that contribute to the overall character or enjoyment of an area. For example, open land, trees, historic buildings and the inter-relationship between them, or less tangible factors such as tranquillity.
Ancient Woodland: An area that has been wooded continuously since at least 1600 AD. It includes ancient semi-natural woodland and plantations on ancient woodland sites (PAWS).
Conservation (for heritage policy): The process of maintaining and managing change to a heritage asset in a way that sustains and, where appropriate, enhances its significance.
Community  Infrastructure  Levy (CIL) *:  A  levy  allowing  local  authorities  to  raise  funds  from owners or developers of land undertaking new building projects in their area.

Development plan: Is defined in section 38 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004, and includes adopted local plans, neighbourhood plans that have been made and published spatial development  strategies,  together  with  any  regional  strategy  policies  that  remain  in  force. Neighbourhood plans that have been approved at referendum are also part of the development plan, unless the local planning authority decides that the neighbourhood plan should not be made.
Economic development *: Development, including those within the B and E Use Classes, public and community uses, and main town centre uses (but excluding housing development).

Green  infrastructure: A  network  of  multi-functional  green  and  blue  spaces  and  other  natural features, urban and rural, which is capable of delivering a wide range of environmental, economic, health and wellbeing benefits for nature, climate, local and wider communities and prosperity.

Heritage asset: A building, monument, site, place, area or landscape identified as having a degree of  significance  meriting  consideration  in  planning  decisions,  because  of  its  heritage  interest. Heritage  asset  includes  designated  heritage  assets  and  assets  identified  by the  local  planning authority (including local listing).

Historic  environment:  All  aspects  of  the  environment  resulting  from  the  interaction  between people and places through time, including all surviving physical remains of past human activity, whether visible, buried or submerged, and landscaped and planted or managed flora.

International,  national  and  locally  designated  sites  of  importance  for  biodiversity:  All international  sites  (Special  Areas of Conservation,  Special Protection  Areas,  and Ramsar  sites),
